questions.question: State Avogadro's law and explain, using the emptiness of gases, why one mole of any gas occupies 22,4 dm³ at STP regardless of its molar mass.
questions.expected_answer: Equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules. A gas is almost entirely empty space, so its volume is set by the spacing between molecules — fixed by temperature and pressure — not by molecular size or mass. At STP (0 °C / 273 K and 101,3 kPa) that spacing gives 22,4 dm³ per mole for every gas, whether hydrogen at 2 g/mol or CO₂ at 44 g/mol.

questions.question: Walk through the 13 g Zn + excess HCl problem, explaining the role of the word 'excess' and where the 22,4 enters the calculation.
questions.expected_answer: Excess means more than enough acid, so all the zinc reacts and the calculation is based on it. Legs: 13 g ÷ 65 g/mol = 0,2 mol Zn; ratio 1 : 1 gives 0,2 mol H₂; V = n × Vm = 0,2 × 22,4 = 4,48 dm³ at STP. The 22,4 enters only at the last leg, converting the product's moles to volume; by mass instead it would be 0,2 × 2 = 0,4 g.

questions.question: In your own words, explain why total gas volume is not conserved in 2CO + O₂ → 2CO₂ although mass is, and when the volume-ratio shortcut may be used.
questions.expected_answer: Three reactant molecules become two product molecules; since equal counts at shared conditions fill equal volumes, 30 dm³ shrinks to 20 dm³ while the mass balances exactly — volume follows molecule count, mass follows atoms. The shortcut (coefficients read as volumes) may be used only when all the substances compared are gases at the same temperature and pressure — not necessarily STP, since the shared crate size cancels from the ratio.
